JP-N4-01-001.notes: だった is the plain past of だ: 雨だった 'it was rain(y)'. Nouns and な-adjectives use だ, じゃない, だった, じゃなかった; with friends these replace です and でした.
JP-N4-01-001.tip: Noun or な-adjective: だ → だった → じゃなかった.

JP-N4-01-002.notes: い-adjectives need no だ in plain speech: おもしろくなかった on its own is a full sentence. Adding だ after an い-adjective (×おもしろいだ) is a typical learner error.
JP-N4-01-002.tip: Never add だ after an い-adjective.

JP-N4-01-003.notes: じゃない is the plain negative of だ: 学生じゃない 'isn't a student'. よ adds 'I'm telling you'. In writing, ではない is preferred.

JP-N4-01-004.notes: な-adjectives take だった in the plain past: しずかだった. ね at the end looks for agreement about a shared experience: we were both there.

JP-N4-01-005.notes: んです after a plain form gives an explanation or background: おくれたんです 'the train was late, you see'. Without it, the sentence would be a bare report.
JP-N4-01-005.tip: んです = 'it's that…', explaining a situation.

JP-N4-01-006.notes: んですか asks for an explanation of what you can see: a friend has a bandage, so どうしたんですか 'what happened?'. Plain どうしましたか is more neutral, as a doctor might say.

JP-N4-01-007.notes: Nouns and な-adjectives take な before んです: 仕事なんです. It's a soft way to refuse: the reason is stated and the refusal itself is left unsaid.
JP-N4-01-007.tip: Noun + なんです: 仕事なんです, not ×仕事だんです.

JP-N4-01-008.notes: と思います after a plain form means 'I think': 雨だと思います. Nouns and な-adjectives need だ before と, though in the main sentence だ would often be dropped.
JP-N4-01-008.tip: Noun + だと思う: 雨だと思う.

JP-N4-01-009.notes: と marks what is thought or said: 来ないと思います. Japanese usually puts the negative in the quoted part ('think he won't come'), where English says 'don't think he will'.

JP-N4-01-010.notes: い-adjectives go straight before と思います: おもしろいと思います. No だ is added, unlike nouns and な-adjectives. The negative is おもしろくないと思います.

JP-N4-01-011.notes: と marks a direct quotation in 「」 brackets: 「…」と言いました. Japanese uses 「」 where English uses inverted commas.

JP-N4-01-012.notes: と言いました with a plain-form clause reports speech indirectly: 来ると言いました 'said he'd come'. The tense inside stays as the speaker said it; there's no backshift.
JP-N4-01-012.tip: No backshift: 来ると言った = said he would come.

JP-N4-01-013.notes: 何と言いますか asks what something is called: 日本語で何と言いますか 'what's it called in Japanese?'. In speech, 何て言いますか is common.

JP-N4-01-014.notes: という links a name to a noun: 「さくら」という店 'a shop called Sakura'. It's used when the listener may not know the name.
JP-N4-01-014.tip: X という + noun = a (noun) called X.

JP-N4-01-015.notes: という after a person's name suggests the speaker doesn't know them: 田中という人 'someone called Tanaka'. Dropping さん is normal here.

JP-N4-01-016.notes: でしょう is polite, as in a weather forecast; だろう is its plain form, used in thinking aloud, diaries and essays, or by men in casual speech. たぶん (probably) often comes with both.
JP-N4-01-016.tip: だろう is the form for diaries, essays and thinking aloud.
JP-N4-01-016.register: でしょう polite; だろう plain or written

JP-N4-01-017.notes: The imperative of a う-verb changes the final -u to -e: 走る → 走れ. It's blunt, heard from coaches, on signs and in emergencies; face to face it sounds harsh.
JP-N4-01-017.tip: Imperatives: 走れ, 起きろ, しろ, 来い.

JP-N4-01-018.notes: る-verbs form the imperative with ろ: 起きる → 起きろ. A parent shouting at a lazy teenager might use it; a gentler alternative is 起きなさい.

JP-N4-01-019.notes: 止まれ, the imperative of 止まる, is printed on Japanese stop signs. Signs and slogans use the blunt imperative because no particular person is being addressed.

JP-N4-01-020.notes: Dictionary form + な is the blunt prohibition: 止めるな 'don't park'. This な is different from the な of な-adjectives and from the sentence-final ね-like な.

JP-N4-01-021.notes: なさい after the verb stem gives a firm instruction from a parent or teacher: 寝なさい 'go to bed'. It's firm but not rude, softer than 寝ろ.

JP-N4-01-022.notes: なさい also appears in exam instructions: 書きなさい 'write'. Between adults it sounds patronising, so 書いてください is used instead.

JP-N4-02-001.notes: The potential of a う-verb changes the final -u to -e + る: 読む → 読める. The object often switches from を to が: 漢字が読める.
JP-N4-02-001.tip: Potential: 読む → 読める; the object often takes が.

JP-N4-02-002.notes: る-verbs form the potential with られる: 食べる → 食べられる. The same form is also the passive, so context decides between 'can eat' and 'be eaten'.

JP-N4-02-003.notes: 話す → 話せる: 'can speak'. 少し (a little) is a modest way to describe your own ability, even when you speak well.

JP-N4-02-004.notes: 来る has the potential 来られる (こられる). In speech, 来れる is very common; this 'ら-dropping' is widespread but still marked as non-standard in exams.
JP-N4-02-004.tip: 来られる is standard; 来れる is common in speech.

JP-N4-02-005.notes: およぐ → およげる → およげません 'can't swim'. ぐ-verbs form the potential like other う-verbs, with -e + る. Swimming as a skill can also be 泳ぐことができます.

JP-N4-02-006.notes: ことができる after the dictionary form means 'can': 使うことができます. It's more formal than the potential 使えます and is typical of notices and announcements.

JP-N4-02-007.notes: ことができる works with any verb: ピアノをひくことができます. With する-nouns, the shorter noun + ができる is used: 運転ができます. ひく is used for keyboards and strings: ピアノをひく, ギターをひく.

JP-N4-02-008.notes: 見える means something is visible by itself (the mountains are in view); 見られる means you are able to see or watch it, given access or a chance.
JP-N4-02-008.tip: 見える = in view; 見られる = can watch.

JP-N4-02-009.notes: 聞こえる means a sound reaches you without effort; 聞ける means you are able to listen, given the means. Music through a wall 聞こえる; music on an app can be 聞ける.

JP-N4-03-001.notes: たら is the plain past + ら: ふった + ら. It's the most flexible conditional: 'if' or 'when', and the main clause can be a decision, request or wish.
JP-N4-03-001.tip: たら = plain past + ら; it works with requests.

JP-N4-03-002.notes: たら for a certain future event means 'when, once': 駅についたら 'when you arrive'. Because the main clause is a request, ば or と wouldn't fit here.

JP-N4-03-003.notes: ある → あった → あったら 'if there is / if I have'. お金がある means 'have money'; the money is the subject with が.

JP-N4-03-004.notes: い-adjectives take かったら: 安い → 安かったら. Nouns and な-adjectives take だったら: 雨だったら, ひまだったら. The main clause states the decision: then I'll buy it.

JP-N4-03-005.notes: ば after a う-verb changes the final -u to -e + ば: なる → なれば. ば suits general truths and conditions; the main clause states what follows naturally.
JP-N4-03-005.tip: ば: final -u → -e + ば (なる → なれば).

JP-N4-03-006.notes: 飲む → 飲めば 'if you take'. ば stresses the condition itself: all you need to do is take this medicine. The negative condition is 飲まなければ: 'unless you take it'.

JP-N4-03-007.notes: ある → あれば 'if there is'. 時間があれば is a stock phrase for a tentative promise: 'if I have time, I'll go'.

JP-N4-03-008.notes: い-adjectives take ければ: 高い → 高ければ. Negative conditions use なければ: 高くなければ 'if it isn't expensive'. Nouns take なら or であれば instead.

JP-N4-03-009.notes: と after the dictionary form describes an automatic result: press the button and the door opens. The main clause can't be a request or an intention.
JP-N4-03-009.tip: と: A always leads to B; no requests after it.

JP-N4-03-010.notes: と for natural, repeated events: 春になると 'whenever spring comes'. It fits facts that happen every time, like seasons and machines.

JP-N4-03-011.notes: と in directions: 右にまがると、駅があります 'turn right and there's the station'. The main clause describes what you find, not an instruction.

JP-N4-03-012.notes: なら takes up what the other person has just said: 'if (it's true that) you're going to Kyoto'. The advice that follows can apply before the trip itself.
JP-N4-03-012.tip: なら replies to what the other person said.

JP-N4-03-013.notes: なら after a noun means 'if it's…, as for…': すしなら 'if it's sushi (you want)'. It picks out the topic and offers a recommendation.

JP-N4-03-014.notes: たら means B happens after A (arrive, then call); なら allows B before A (take the bullet train to get to Kyoto). Order in time decides.
JP-N4-03-014.tip: たら: A first, then B; なら: B can come first.

JP-N4-03-015.notes: ばよかった expresses regret: 来ればよかった 'I should have come'. Literally 'if I had come, it would have been good'. たらよかった says the same.
JP-N4-03-015.tip: ばよかった = should have; なければよかった = shouldn't have.

JP-N4-03-016.notes: 持ってくる (bring) → 持ってくれば → 持ってくればよかった. くる is irregular, but its ば form looks regular: くれば. The て-form of 持つ, 持って, joins to it.

JP-N4-03-017.notes: なければよかった means 'shouldn't have': 言わなければよかった. The ない form changes い to ければ: 言わない → 言わなければ. The regret is about something actually said.

JP-N4-03-018.notes: たらどうですか suggests an action: 休んだらどうですか 'why don't you rest?'. To a superior it can sound pushy; たらいかがですか is politer.
JP-N4-03-018.tip: To a superior: 〜たらいかがですか.

JP-N4-03-019.notes: ばいいですか asks for advice: 買えばいいですか 'where should I buy?'. The answer often uses the same pattern: 駅で買えばいいですよ.

JP-N4-04-001.notes: The volitional of a う-verb changes the final -u to -o + う: 帰る → 帰ろう. It's the casual 'let's', equal to 帰りましょう.
JP-N4-04-001.tip: Volitional: 帰る → 帰ろう; 食べる → 食べよう.

JP-N4-04-002.notes: る-verbs take よう: 食べる → 食べよう. Adding か (食べようか) turns it into 'shall we…?' among friends. The polite equivalent is 食べましょうか.

JP-N4-04-003.notes: 休む → 休もう 'let's rest'. 少し softens the suggestion: just a short break. The ます-form equivalent, 休みましょう, would suit colleagues.

JP-N4-04-004.notes: Volitional + と思っています means 'I'm thinking of doing': 行こうと思っています. ている shows the idea has been around for a while.
JP-N4-04-004.tip: ようと思っている = an ongoing plan; ようと思う = a thought now.

JP-N4-04-005.notes: Volitional + と思います can show a decision made on the spot: 買おうと思います 'I think I'll buy'. 買う → 買おう. The decision is fresh, not long considered.

JP-N4-04-006.notes: つもり after the dictionary form means 'intend to': 行くつもりです. It's firmer than 行こうと思っています. Asking a superior つもりですか can sound like a challenge.
JP-N4-04-006.tip: Don't ask superiors つもりですか; it sounds challenging.

JP-N4-04-007.notes: ないつもり means 'intend not to': すわないつもりです. もう + negative means 'no longer': I won't smoke any more. It states a resolution, like a New Year's promise.

JP-N4-04-008.notes: 予定 after the dictionary form means 'scheduled to': 始まる予定です. It's an arrangement already fixed, not just an intention.
JP-N4-04-008.tip: 予定 = scheduled; つもり = intended.

JP-N4-04-009.notes: 予定 after a noun takes の: 旅行の予定です 'a trip is planned'. 来週は sets next week apart as the topic. With a verb: 旅行する予定です.

JP-N4-04-010.notes: ことにする means 'decide to' (your own choice); ことになる means 'it's been decided' (by others or circumstances). Japanese often uses ことになる even for your own choices, to sound modest.
JP-N4-04-010.tip: ことにする = I decide; ことになる = it's been decided.
JP-N4-04-010.register: Polite (ます); ことになる common in announcements

JP-N4-04-011.notes: ことにしました reports a decision you made yourself: 'I've decided to keep a diary'. ことにしています means it has become your rule.

JP-N4-04-012.notes: ようになる after a potential form shows a gradual change in ability: 話せるようになりました 'have become able to speak'. It's the natural way to report progress.
JP-N4-04-012.tip: Potential + ようになる = can now (after a change).

JP-N4-04-013.notes: ようになる after a dictionary form shows a new habit: 食べるようになりました 'I've started eating'. The change happened over time, not overnight.

JP-N4-04-014.notes: ようにしています means 'make a point of': 早くねるようにしています. It's an effort you keep up, not a fixed rule. Typical with health habits: sleep, exercise, diet.
JP-N4-04-014.tip: ようにする = make an effort; ようになる = a change that happens.

JP-N4-04-015.notes: ないようにしています means 'try not to': 食べないようにしています. It's softer than 食べません and admits the effort may fail. あまいもの = sweet things.

JP-N4-04-016.notes: にする after a noun means 'choose, go for': カレーにします 'I'll have the curry'. It's the standard way to order in a restaurant or pick from options.
JP-N4-04-016.text: (Ordering) 私はカレー{{c1::にします::decide on / choose}}。
JP-N4-04-016.flag: dup: replaced 私はコーヒーにします (near-identical to N5-01-014)

JP-N4-04-017.notes: にしました reports a choice made: 来月にしました 'we've settled on next month'. にする works for dates, colours and sizes as well as food.

JP-N4-04-018.notes: くする means someone makes it so (I turned it up); くなる means it became so by itself. い-adjectives take く; な-adjectives and nouns take に.
JP-N4-04-018.tip: する = someone makes it so; なる = it becomes so.

JP-N4-04-019.notes: 小さい → 小さくする 'make smaller, turn down'. With volume, 大きくする is turn up and 小さくする turn down. Compare 音が小さくなった: it went quiet by itself.

JP-N4-04-020.notes: な-adjectives take に + する: きれいにする 'make clean, tidy'. A する-change always has a person behind it. Compare へやがきれいになった: no agent implied.

JP-N4-05-001.notes: てしまう has two senses: doing something completely, or doing it with regret. With ぜんぶ (all), やってしまいました means 'have got it all done'.
JP-N4-05-001.tip: てしまう = completely, or regrettably.

JP-N4-05-002.notes: てしまう with an accident shows regret: なくしてしまいました 'I've (gone and) lost it'. Plain なくしました would be a neutral report.

JP-N4-05-003.notes: ちゃう is the casual contraction of てしまう: 食べてしまった → 食べちゃった. With む, ぶ, ぬ and ぐ verbs it's じゃう: 飲んじゃった. The tone is light, often apologetic.
JP-N4-05-003.tip: てしまう → ちゃう; でしまう → じゃう.

JP-N4-05-004.notes: ておく means doing something in advance, as preparation: 買っておきます 'buy beforehand'. The reason (before the party) is often stated.
JP-N4-05-004.tip: ておく = do in advance; casual とく.

JP-N4-05-005.notes: ておいた reports preparation done: 予約しておきました 'I'd booked a hotel in advance'. With する-verbs: しておく. The booking was done ahead, in readiness.

JP-N4-05-006.notes: ておく also means 'leave as it is': あけておいてください 'leave it open'. The window was already open and should stay that way.

JP-N4-05-007.notes: てみる means 'try doing, to see what it's like': 食べてみたい 'want to try eating'. It's not 'attempt'; for that, ようとする is used.
JP-N4-05-007.tip: てみる = try out; ようとする = attempt.

JP-N4-05-008.notes: 着てみます means 'try on' clothes: test them by wearing. The verb for clothes depends on the body part: 着る (top), はく (bottom), かぶる (head).

JP-N4-05-009.notes: 行ってみました means 'went to try out', to see what the new shop was like. The place takes に as the destination of 行く.

JP-N4-05-010.notes: てある after a transitive verb (あける) means someone did it on purpose and the result remains. ている after an intransitive verb (あく) just describes the state.
JP-N4-05-010.tip: Transitive + てある = left that way on purpose.

JP-N4-05-011.notes: はってあります: someone has put the calendar up, and there it is. The thing takes が, not を, with てある. The noun has been put up and left in place.

JP-N4-05-012.notes: おいてあります: someone has left a note on the desk, presumably for you. おく means 'put, place'; ておく is a different pattern.

JP-N4-05-013.notes: ていく shows change from now into the future; てくる shows change up to now. The direction words 'go' and 'come' map onto time.
JP-N4-05-013.tip: ていく = from now on; てくる = up to now.

JP-N4-05-014.notes: てくる can also mean 'go, do and come back': 買ってきます 'I'll go and buy some'. It's a typical announcement as you leave the room.

JP-N4-05-015.notes: なくてもいい means 'don't have to': 来なくてもいいです. The ない form drops い and adds くてもいい: 来ない → 来なくても. The opposite is 来なければなりません (must come).
JP-N4-05-015.tip: なくてもいい = don't have to.

JP-N4-05-016.notes: ぬがなくてもいいです 'you don't need to take your shoes off'. ぬぐ is used for removing clothes and shoes. Removing a hat uses とる; glasses, はずす.

JP-N4-05-017.notes: なければなりません means 'must, have to': 起きなければなりません. It's formal and long; speech prefers なきゃ or なくちゃ. The prohibition てはいけない is its opposite.
JP-N4-05-017.tip: Must: なければならない; casual なきゃ / なくちゃ.

JP-N4-05-018.notes: 飲まなければなりません 'I have to take'. The ない form 飲まない changes い to ければ. なければいけません means the same. The obligation here is medical, from outside.

JP-N4-05-019.notes: なきゃ is the casual form of なければ, with the rest of the sentence dropped: 帰らなきゃ (いけない). It's common when leaving.

JP-N4-05-020.notes: たほうがいい after the past form gives advice: 飲んだほうがいい 'you'd better take'. The past form is used even though the advice is about the future.
JP-N4-05-020.tip: Advice: past form + ほうがいい.

JP-N4-05-021.notes: ないほうがいい means 'you'd better not': 飲まないほうがいい. The negative uses the present ない form, not the past. あまり + negative here means 'not too much'.

JP-N4-05-022.notes: てほしい with に + person means 'want someone to do': 母に来てほしい. With a superior it sounds demanding; ていただきたい is the polite version.
JP-N4-05-022.tip: To superiors: 〜ていただきたいです.

JP-N4-05-023.notes: 友だちに話してほしい 'want my friend to talk'. The person you want to act takes に; the wish is yours. The verb is in the て-form before ほしい.

JP-N4-06-001.notes: あげる: I give to others. くれる: others give to me or my group. もらう: I receive. The direction of giving decides the verb, not just who gives.
JP-N4-06-001.tip: あげる = away from me; くれる = towards me; もらう = I receive.
JP-N4-06-001.text:
私は友だちに本を{{c1::あげました::あげる / くれる / もらう?}}。
友だちは私に本を{{c2::くれました::あげる / くれる / もらう?}}。
私は友だちに本を{{c3::もらいました::あげる / くれる / もらう?}}。
JP-N4-06-001.flag: hint: added '?' to the option list so the card counts as Choice

JP-N4-06-002.notes: くれる is used when the receiver is in the speaker's group: 妹にくれました. My sister counts as 'my side', so あげる would be wrong.
JP-N4-06-002.text: 田中さんは妹にお菓子を{{c1::くれました::あげる / くれる / もらう?}}。
JP-N4-06-002.flag: hint: added '?' to the option list so the card counts as Choice

JP-N4-06-003.notes: いただく is the humble form of もらう, used when receiving from a superior: 先生にいただきました. The giver takes に or から.

JP-N4-06-004.notes: くださる is the honorific of くれる: a superior gives to my side. Its ます form is irregular: くださいます, not ×くださります.
JP-N4-06-004.tip: くださる → くださいます (irregular ます form).
JP-N4-06-004.text: 社長が私たちにお菓子を{{c1::くださいました::くれる · honorific}}。
JP-N4-06-004.tr: The company president gave us some sweets.
JP-N4-06-004.flag: dup: replaced 先生が本をくださいました (near-identical to N4-06-003)

JP-N4-06-005.notes: てあげる means doing a favour for someone else: 手伝ってあげました. Said directly to a superior, it can sound condescending.
JP-N4-06-005.tip: Avoid てあげる towards superiors.
JP-N4-06-005.text: 弟の宿題を{{c1::手伝ってあげました::手伝う · あげる / くれる / もらう?}}。
JP-N4-06-005.flag: hint: added '?' to the option list so the card counts as Choice

JP-N4-06-006.notes: てくれる means someone did a favour for me: 送ってくれました. It adds gratitude that plain 送りました lacks. 送る means both 'send' and 'see someone off, take them'.
JP-N4-06-006.text: 友だちが駅まで{{c1::送ってくれました::送る · あげる / くれる / もらう?}}。
JP-N4-06-006.flag: hint: added '?' to the option list so the card counts as Choice

JP-N4-06-007.notes: てもらう means I got someone to do something: 教えてもらいました. The helper takes に. It stresses the receiver's gratitude.
JP-N4-06-007.text: 田中さんに日本語を{{c1::教えてもらいました::教える · あげる / くれる / もらう?}}。
JP-N4-06-007.flag: hint: added '?' to the option list so the card counts as Choice

JP-N4-07-001.notes: そう after an adjective stem means 'looks': おいしい → おいしそう 'looks delicious'. It's a judgement from appearance, before tasting.
JP-N4-07-001.tip: Looks: い-adjective minus い + そう.

JP-N4-07-002.notes: な-adjectives take そう directly: 元気そう 'looks well'. Nouns can't take this そう; for them, みたい or のようだ is used. おばあちゃん is a familiar word for grandma.
JP-N4-07-002.text: おばあちゃんはとても{{c1::元気そうです::元気 · looks}}。
JP-N4-07-002.flag: dup: replaced 田中さんは元気そうです (near-identical to N4-07-005)

JP-N4-07-003.notes: いい is irregular: よさそう 'looks good', with さ inserted. ない likewise becomes なさそう. The polite question is よさそうですね.
JP-N4-07-003.tip: いい → よさそう; ない → なさそう.

JP-N4-07-004.notes: Stem + そう means 'looks about to' from what you see; plain form + そう means 'I hear' from someone else. ふりそう vs ふるそう.
JP-N4-07-004.tip: Stem + そう = looks like; plain + そう = I hear.

JP-N4-07-005.notes: そうです after a plain form reports hearsay: 結婚するそうです 'I hear he's getting married'. The source can be added with によると.

JP-N4-07-006.notes: おいしいそうです 'I hear it's good', reporting someone else's view. Compare おいしそうです, 'it looks good', from your own eyes.

JP-N4-07-007.notes: ようです after a plain form means 'it seems', judging from what you see or sense: the lights are off, so he's gone home.
JP-N4-07-007.tip: ようだ = from your own observation.

JP-N4-07-008.notes: ふったようです: the wet street is evidence that it rained. ようだ admits the conclusion is an inference, not a direct observation.

JP-N4-07-009.notes: みたい is the casual form of ようだ: かぜをひいたみたい 'I think I've caught a cold'. Nouns take it directly: 雨みたい.
JP-N4-07-009.tip: みたい = casual ようだ.

JP-N4-07-010.notes: のように after a noun means 'like': 日本人のように 'like a Japanese person'. Casual speech uses みたいに. As a predicate: 日本人のようです 'seems Japanese'. It describes manner here.

JP-N4-07-011.notes: らしい after a plain form means 'apparently', based on something heard or read. It's less direct than そうです and keeps the speaker at a distance.
JP-N4-07-011.tip: らしい = from what I've heard or read.

JP-N4-07-012.notes: らしい after a noun can mean 'typical of, true to type': 春らしい 'really spring-like'. This sense has nothing to do with hearsay.

JP-N4-07-013.notes: はずです means 'should, is expected to', based on reasoning: he said three o'clock, so he should come at three.
JP-N4-07-013.tip: はず = what reason leads you to expect.

JP-N4-07-014.notes: あるはずです 'should be there': you remember putting the key in the bag. はずがない reverses it: 'there's no way'.

JP-N4-07-015.notes: かもしれません means 'might, perhaps': ふるかもしれません. It's less confident than でしょう. The ending can be 雨がふるかもしれません or, casually, ふるかも.
JP-N4-07-015.tip: かもしれない is less sure than でしょう.

JP-N4-07-016.notes: Nouns and な-adjectives take かもしれない directly, without だ: 先生かもしれません. ×先生だかもしれません is wrong. The speaker isn't sure who they are.

JP-N4-07-017.notes: かもしれない after a past form means 'might have': 帰ったかもしれない. In casual speech it's often cut to かも. The polite form is 帰ったかもしれません.

JP-N4-07-018.notes: がる turns a feeling adjective into a verb about someone else: ほしい → ほしがる. ている is used for a current wish: ほしがっています.
JP-N4-07-018.tip: Others' feelings: ほしがる, こわがる, 行きたがる.

JP-N4-07-019.notes: こわい → こわがる 'be scared (as others see it)'. The thing feared takes を with がる, not が. The noun form is こわがり (a scaredy-cat).

JP-N4-07-020.notes: たがる after a verb stem describes a third person's wish: 行きたがっています. 妹は行きたいです would wrongly claim to know her mind directly.

JP-N4-08-001.notes: The passive of a る-verb uses られる: ほめる → ほめられる. The doer takes に: 先生にほめられました. Being praised is a positive passive; the passive isn't always negative.
JP-N4-08-001.tip: Passive: doer + に + られる / れる.

JP-N4-08-002.notes: う-verbs form the passive with -a + れる: 読む → 読まれる. ている shows a continuing state: is (widely) read. The doer here is many people: たくさんの人に.

JP-N4-08-003.notes: The 'suffering passive' shows the subject was affected badly: 弟にケーキを食べられました 'my brother ate my cake (on me)'. English has no direct equivalent.
JP-N4-08-003.tip: Suffering passive: something was done to you or yours.

JP-N4-08-004.notes: 雨にふられました literally 'was rained on': an intransitive verb in the passive, a pure 'suffering' use. English says 'got caught in the rain'.

JP-N4-08-005.notes: The causative of a る-verb uses させる: 食べる → 食べさせる 'make (someone) eat'. The person made to act takes に here because there's an object (野菜を).

JP-N4-08-006.notes: う-verbs form the causative with -a + せる: 走る → 走らせる. With an intransitive verb like 走る, the person made to act usually takes を: 選手たちを走らせる.
JP-N4-08-006.text: コーチは選手たちを{{c1::走らせました::走る · make (someone) do}}。
JP-N4-08-006.tr: The coach made the players run.
JP-N4-08-006.flag: dup: replaced 先生は学生に作文を書かせました (near-identical to N4-08-008); answer 書かせました → 走らせました

JP-N4-08-007.notes: させてください asks permission politely: 'please let me (do it)'. 行かせてください 'let me go'. It's common at work: 休ませてください.

JP-N4-08-008.notes: Passive (られる / れる): something is done to the subject. Causative (させる / せる): the subject makes someone else act. The teacher made them read (causative); the student was scolded (passive).

JP-N4-09-001.notes: とき after a dictionary form means 'when (before) A happens'; after a past form 'when (after) A has happened'. 行くとき = on the way; 行ったとき = once there.
JP-N4-09-001.tip: Tense before とき shows the order of events.

JP-N4-09-002.notes: Nouns take の before とき: 子どものとき 'when I was a child'. The tense comes at the end of the sentence (泳ぎました), not inside the とき clause.

JP-N4-09-003.notes: な-adjectives take な before とき: ひまなとき 'when I'm free'. い-adjectives go straight before it: いそがしいとき. The tense of the sentence comes at the end.

JP-N4-09-004.notes: ので gives a reason in a soft, objective tone. Nouns and な-adjectives take な: 休みなので. It suits polite explanations better than から.
JP-N4-09-004.tip: Noun + なので: 休みなので.

JP-N4-09-005.notes: ので before a request sounds polite and reasonable: 頭がいたいので、帰ってもいいですか. から here could sound like a demand.

JP-N4-09-006.notes: から can end a sentence as an answer to 'why?': いそがしかったからです. ので can't: ×のでです. That's why only から fits here.
JP-N4-09-006.tip: Only から can stand before です at the end.

JP-N4-09-007.notes: のに means 'even though', with disappointment or frustration: studied hard, yet failed. It's emotional; けど would be neutral.
JP-N4-09-007.tip: のに = even though (and I'm disappointed).

JP-N4-09-008.notes: Nouns take な before のに: 日曜日なのに 'even though it's Sunday'. The speaker resents having to work. In writing: 日曜日であるにもかかわらず.

JP-N4-09-009.notes: 約束したのに: he promised, yet didn't come. のに often expresses complaint about someone else's behaviour. The complaint is directed at Tanaka.

JP-N4-09-010.notes: し lists reasons, with more implied: 安いし、おいしいし 'it's cheap, and good, and…'. The conclusion follows: so I come often.
JP-N4-09-010.tip: し lists reasons: A し、B し、(so) C.

JP-N4-09-011.notes: し after だ with a noun: 雨だし. A single し can give one reason while hinting at others. The conclusion is stated after the reasons: I don't want to go out.

JP-N4-09-012.notes: ために expresses purpose with a controllable action: 働くために. ように goes with potential forms and outcomes you can't fully control: 話せるように.
JP-N4-09-012.tip: ために + action; ように + potential or ない form.

JP-N4-09-013.notes: ように with a negative: かぜをひかないように 'so as not to catch a cold'. Catching a cold isn't something you do on purpose, so ために won't fit.

JP-N4-09-014.notes: ために with a dictionary form and the same subject: 家を買うために 'to buy a house'. Saving is a deliberate step towards it.

JP-N4-09-015.notes: まで means 'until': the action continues up to five. までに means 'by': the action happens once, at some point before five.
JP-N4-09-015.tip: まで = until; までに = by (a deadline).

JP-N4-09-016.notes: までに sets a deadline: 金曜日までに 'by Friday'. Handing in is a one-off action, so まで alone would be wrong.

JP-N4-09-017.notes: ながら after a verb stem means 'while': 聞きながら勉強する. The main action comes last; the ながら action is the background.
JP-N4-09-017.tip: ながら: background action first, main action last.

JP-N4-09-018.notes: 見ながら食べます 'eat while watching'. Both actions must have the same subject; for two people, 間 or とき is used.

JP-N4-09-019.notes: のに after a dictionary form can mean 'for (the purpose of)', with verbs like 使う, いい and 必要: 切るのに使う 'use for cutting'. This is not the 'even though' のに.
JP-N4-09-019.tip: Purpose のに: with 使う, 便利, 必要, かかる.

JP-N4-10-001.notes: たり…たりする lists example actions: 読んだり、見たりします 'do things like reading and watching'. The final する carries the tense and politeness.
JP-N4-10-001.tip: たり…たりする: examples, ending with する.

JP-N4-10-002.notes: したり after する-verbs: 買い物をしたり. The list isn't complete; other activities are implied. そうじをする = do the cleaning.

JP-N4-10-003.notes: たことがある after a past form means 'have done (at least once)': 行ったことがあります 'have been to'. It refers to experience, not a recent event.
JP-N4-10-003.tip: たことがある = have the experience of.

JP-N4-10-004.notes: たことがありません 'have never': 食べたことがありません. To say 'not yet' about something expected, まだ…ていません is used instead.

JP-N4-10-005.notes: たことがありますか asks about experience: 'have you ever…?'. 運転する = drive. The answer is はい、あります or いいえ、ありません.
JP-N4-10-005.text: 外国で{{c1::運転したことがありますか::運転する · have you ever?}}。
JP-N4-10-005.flag: dup: replaced 富士山に登ったことがありますか (same sentence as part of N4-10-026); answer 登ったことがありますか → 運転したことがありますか

JP-N4-10-006.notes: A plain-form clause goes straight before the noun it describes: 私が作ったケーキ 'the cake I made'. There's no word for 'that' or 'which'.
JP-N4-10-006.tip: Relative clause = plain form + noun; no 'that'.

JP-N4-10-007.notes: 昨日会った人 'the person I met yesterday'. The verb in the clause is in the plain past; the sentence's politeness sits on the final です.

JP-N4-10-008.notes: めがねをかけている人 'the person wearing glasses'. めがねをかける is 'wear glasses'; ている describes the state. Each item of clothing has its own verb: 着る, はく, かぶる, かける.

JP-N4-10-009.notes: Negative and potential forms can also describe nouns: 話せない人 'people who can't speak'. も after the noun means 'also, some'.

JP-N4-10-010.notes: かどうか embeds a yes/no question: 来るかどうか 'whether or not he'll come'. With a question word (何時), plain か alone is used.
JP-N4-10-010.tip: Yes/no inside a sentence: かどうか; with a question word: か.

JP-N4-10-011.notes: すぎる after a verb stem means 'too much': 飲みすぎました 'drank too much'. It conjugates as a る-verb. The noun form is 飲みすぎ: 飲みすぎに注意 (beware of drinking too much).
JP-N4-10-011.tip: すぎる conjugates as a る-verb: すぎます, すぎた.

JP-N4-10-012.notes: い-adjectives drop い before すぎる: 高い → 高すぎる 'too expensive'. いい becomes よすぎる. Polite: 高すぎます. The negative すぎない means 'not too'.

JP-N4-10-013.notes: な-adjectives take すぎる directly: かんたんすぎる 'too easy'. The nuance is negative: more than is wanted. Compare かんたんです (simple), a neutral description.

JP-N4-10-014.notes: やすい after a verb stem means 'easy to': 書きやすい. It conjugates like an い-adjective: 書きやすくない. The opposite is 書きにくい.
JP-N4-10-014.tip: Stem + やすい = easy to; stem + にくい = hard to.

JP-N4-10-015.notes: にくい after a verb stem means 'hard to': 読みにくい. 小さくて gives the reason: the print is small, so it's hard to read.

JP-N4-10-016.notes: 方 after a verb stem makes 'the way of doing': 使い方 'how to use'. The object takes の, not を: はしの使い方. The same pattern gives 作り方 (recipe, how to make) and 行き方 (how to get there).
JP-N4-10-016.tip: Stem + 方 = how to; object + の, not を.

JP-N4-10-017.notes: 読み方 'way of reading': 漢字の読み方 is a kanji's reading. 方 here is read かた, not ほう. Kanji usually have more than one reading.

JP-N4-10-018.notes: 始める after a verb stem means 'start doing': ふり始める 'start to rain'. 出す (ふり出す) is similar but suggests suddenness.
JP-N4-10-018.tip: Stem + 始める = start; + 終わる = finish; + 続ける = keep on.

JP-N4-10-019.notes: 終わる after a verb stem means 'finish doing': 読み終わる. 読んでしまった adds a sense of completion or regret, but 読み終わった simply states it.

JP-N4-10-020.notes: 続ける after a verb stem means 'keep on doing': 歩き続ける. The length of time comes before it without a particle: 二時間.

JP-N4-10-021.notes: しか + negative stresses that something is too little: ひらがなしか読めません 'can only read hiragana'. だけ is a neutral 'only' with any verb.
JP-N4-10-021.tip: しか always takes a negative verb.

JP-N4-10-022.notes: しかありません 'there's only': 百円しかありません. しか replaces が; ×百円がしか is wrong. The meaning is 'only 100 yen, which isn't enough'. With だけ it would just state the amount: 百円だけあります.

JP-N4-10-023.notes: でも after a noun softens a suggestion: お茶でも 'tea or something'. The speaker leaves the choice open. The verb follows as an invitation.
JP-N4-10-023.tip: Noun + でも softens an invitation.

JP-N4-10-024.notes: でも after a noun can mean 'even': 子どもでもわかる 'even a child would understand'. It implies the thing is easy.

JP-N4-10-025.notes: でも after a question word means 'any-': 何でも (anything), だれでも (anyone), いつでも (any time). With a positive verb.

JP-N4-10-026.notes: Dictionary form + ことがある means 'sometimes do'; past form + ことがある means 'have done'. The tense before こと decides.
JP-N4-10-026.tip: Dictionary + ことがある = sometimes; past + ことがある = have done.

JP-N4-10-027.notes: ないことがある 'sometimes don't': 食べないことがあります. It's milder than ときどき食べません and implies it's not the norm. The ない form + ことがある.

JP-N4-11-001.notes: いらっしゃる is the honorific for 行く, 来る and いる. Its ます form is irregular: いらっしゃいます, not ×いらっしゃります. 社長 = company president; the subject is a superior.
JP-N4-11-001.tip: いらっしゃる → いらっしゃいます.

JP-N4-11-002.notes: おっしゃる is the honorific for 言う: 何とおっしゃいましたか 'what did you say?' (to a superior). Its ます form is おっしゃいます.

JP-N4-11-003.notes: めしあがる is the honorific for 食べる and 飲む: どうぞめしあがってください 'please help yourself'. Hosts say it when offering food.

JP-N4-11-004.notes: いらっしゃいます here replaces います, for a superior's location. The same verb covers being, coming and going, so context decides.

JP-N4-11-005.notes: なさる is the honorific for する: ゴルフをなさいます. Like くださる and いらっしゃる, its ます form uses い: なさいます. なさる is also used in shops: 何になさいますか.

JP-N4-11-006.notes: お + stem + になる is the general honorific pattern: 帰る → お帰りになる. It's used for verbs without a special honorific form.
JP-N4-11-006.tip: General honorific: お + stem + になる.

JP-N4-11-007.notes: お読みになりましたか 'have you read?' (to a superior). The person addressed is the subject, raised by the honorific.

JP-N4-11-008.notes: まいる is the humble form of 行く and 来る: そちらへまいります. Humble verbs lower your own actions; they're never used for the listener.
JP-N4-11-008.tip: Humble verbs describe your own actions.

JP-N4-11-009.notes: もうす (申す) is the humble form of 言う: 田中ともうします 'my name is Tanaka'. Dropping さん from your own name is essential.

JP-N4-11-010.notes: いたす is the humble form of する: ご案内いたします 'I'll show you round'. ご + kanji noun + いたす is the humble pattern for する-nouns.

JP-N4-11-011.notes: おる is the humble form of いる: 会社におります. It's common on the phone and in business: 田中はただいま席を外しております. The plain いる would sound too casual.

JP-N4-11-012.notes: お + stem + する is the general humble pattern: 持つ → お持ちする 'let me carry'. It describes something you do for the other person.
JP-N4-11-012.tip: General humble: お + stem + する.

JP-N4-11-013.notes: ご or お + する-noun + する: お電話します 'I'll call you'. 電話 takes お despite being a kanji word, by custom. Similarly お手紙, お約束.

JP-N4-11-014.notes: Honorific (いらっしゃる) raises other people's actions; humble (まいる) lowers your own. One verb, 来る, needs a different form depending on who comes.
JP-N4-11-014.tip: Others' actions → honorific; your own → humble.
